propofol anesthesia does not produce persistent spatial memory deficits in aged rats, whereas isoflur-ane anesthesia does.

(1) the aged rat is an appropriate model of human postoperative cognitive dysfunction (POCD); (2) the choice of general anesthetic can affect the development of POCD; and (3) the mechanism of anesthesia is a critical determinant of the effect of anesthesia on the aged brain.

the state of anesthesia per se is not necessary or sufficient for the development of postanesthesia memory impairment, and that the choice of anesthetic may influence late cognitive outcome in aged subjects.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effects of anesthesia on cognitive function are dependent on both the state of the patient and the specific agent used.
the state of anesthesia is neither necessary for, nor sufficient to cause, postoperative cognitive dysfunction.
the state of anesthesia is neither necessary, nor sufficient, for development of post-anesthetic cognitive impairment, however, the type of anesthetic may be important.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the anesthetic agent and age are important determinants of cognitive outcome after anesthesia.
the anesthetic state per se does not appear to be necessary or sufficient to cause memory impairment, but that the choice of anesthetic may play an important role in late cognitive outcomes.

the choice of general anesthetics for aged patients may be important, and that the state of anesthetized unconsciousness is neither necessary nor a sufficient condition for the development of postanesthesia cognitive impairment.
The main takeaway from our work is that
propofol anesthesia does not cause persistent cognitive deficits in the aged.
we should not be using anesthetics in the elderly that we know have persistent cognitive effects, like nitrous oxide and isofluranes.
we should be cautious in our choice of anesthetics for the elderly.
